newsitem.title: USA: U.S. motorists to enjoy cheaper summer gasoline.
newsitem.headline: U.S. motorists to enjoy cheaper summer gasoline.

text.p: When U.S. motorists hit the road this summer, they'll have more money for fun as flat demand and cheaper crude oil keep pump prices lower than a year ago.
A year-to-date drop in gasoline prices has analysts and consumer groups optimistic that prices could be two to five cents a gallon cheaper than last summer.
The forecasts come as millions of Americans kick off the summer vacation season this Memorial Day weekend, the traditional start of heavier driving in the United States.
American drivers have seen the average price of regular unleaded self-serve gasoline drop 4.5 cents since March, compared with a 17.8 cent jump a year earlier.

"The overall feeling is that gas prices are hospitable to auto travel," said Mike Morrisey, spokesman for the American Automobile Association (AAA), which monitors pump prices for its auto club members.
AAA forecasts the average May gasoline price will be $1.24 a gallon versus $1.31 a year ago.
The cheaper prices come as a relief to Americans, 82 percent of whom vacation by car, according to Travel Industry Association of America.
"This year, we don't get the call from members. They're not as worried about prices. That's clear," AAA's Morrisey said.
Prices have loosened up amid forecasts of flat demand, strong refinery production and, most important, a drop in world crude prices.
"No other factor even comes close," said Trilby Lundberg, head of California-based Lundberg Letter, which surveys retail gasoline prices.
The price of West Texas Intermediate/Cushing crude, a U.S benchmark grade, has averaged about $19.78 a barrel since March against $21.66 in the same period last year, according to analysts.
A low number of refinery fires and shutdowns, which plagued gas production last spring, should also put a lid on summer prices.
"The absence of (refinery) problems would be another reason prices have been softening throughout this year. This is the fifth consecutive month of price declines nationwide," said Lundberg.
Ready supplies will also be aided by flat to slightly higher demand.
U.S. gasoline demand in 1997 is expected to rise a mere 0.3 percent to 7.9 million barrels per day.
And the Travel Industry Association says about 230 million trips will be taken this summer, up only two percent from last year.
But some analysts see dark clouds in the otherwise blue skies of summer.
Leaner inventories, a result of the industry's new strategy to cut storage costs, has drawn down gasoline by seven million barrels compared with last year.

"Potentially for consumers it is a dangerous situation because if there is a problem...the market sets itself up for a spike," said Gerry Samuels, managing director of ARB Oil Inc., a energy brokerage firm.
A smaller amount of gas in storage enables big oil companies to pass some savings to consumers, analysts say.
Ed Rothschild, director of consumer group Citizen Action, says that, unless major refineries shut or supply is disrupted in the heavily productive Middle East, prices should stay stable this summer.
"If you're talking about vacations. I dont' think consumers should worry about gasoline...I would say, take that trip to the beach," Rothschild said.
